title: Claude for Agency Operations: the plug-and-play system that replaces junior ops work (SOPs, onboarding, capacity)

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.html:
Most agency onboarding lives in a stack of separate Claude projects, one per deliverable. A human shuttles a Google Form export between them, runs each chat, edits, and saves to Google Docs. The work is simple. That is exactly why it drains you: it is too repetitive to think about and too important to skip.

At two clients a week with 30 to 50 minutes per onboarding, you lose roughly a full work-month every year to data entry. The fix is one prompt set that takes the intake form once and returns all five first-cut documents in a single pass, ready for you to tweak and approve.

The goal is a first cut so close to done that your edit time drops from 50 minutes to under 10. Your job shrinks to approving drafts.

sections.title: How the stack runs (the 4-step loop)
sections.html:
This is the whole operating loop. No code required to start.

  1. Capture once. Client fills your existing Google Form. You export or copy the answers into one variable block.
  2. Run the stack. Paste the intake into a single Claude project that holds all five prompts. Run them top to bottom. Every document comes out in the client's context, not a generic template.
  3. Tweak and approve. You edit the first cut, which now lands at 80 to 90 percent done. You approve.
  4. Feed the wins back. Paste your best approved outputs back into the project as reference examples. The next client's first cut starts from a higher floor.
Step 4 is the part most agencies skip, and it is the one that compounds. Every approved document you save as an example makes the next one sharper. The system trains on your taste.

sections.title: The 5 prompts (paste-ready)
sections.html:
Each block takes the same {{INTAKE}} variable. Drop your form answers into one shared block at the top of the project, or paste them inline. Replace anything in {{...}}.

1. Client Fundamentals

You are an agency strategist writing the Client Fundamentals doc for a new account.

INTAKE FORM ANSWERS:
{{INTAKE}}


Produce a clean Markdown document with these sections:

  1. Client Name & Website
  2. One-line positioning (who they help and the outcome)
  3. Target Audience (job titles, company size, industry, where they gather)
  4. Top 3 Problems Solved (in the client's own language, pulled from the intake)
  5. Proof & Differentiators (case studies, numbers, credentials present in the intake)
  6. Voice notes (3 adjectives + 2 phrases the client actually uses)

Rules:

  • Only use facts present in the intake. Where a field is missing, write "GAP: [what to ask]".
  • No filler, no adjectives you cannot source from the intake.
  • Keep each section to 4 lines or fewer.

2. Action Brief

You are an account director setting the first 90 days for a new client.

CLIENT FUNDAMENTALS:
{{FUNDAMENTALS}}


INTAKE FORM ANSWERS:
{{INTAKE}}


Write a 30/60/90-day Action Brief as a table with columns: Window | Objective | Owner | Deliverable | Success Metric.


Constraints:

  • 2 to 3 rows per window, 6 to 9 total.
  • Every objective ties to a problem listed in the Client Fundamentals.
  • Metrics must be countable (posts shipped, DMs sent, calls booked), never vague.
  • End with one line: "Biggest risk to this plan and the early signal to watch for."

3. LinkedIn Branding (Headline + About)

You are a LinkedIn ghostwriter for a B2B founder.

CLIENT FUNDAMENTALS:
{{FUNDAMENTALS}}


Produce:
A) Three headline options (under 220 characters each). Each leads with the audience and the outcome, no buzzwords.
B) One About section (1,800 to 2,200 characters) in first person, structured as:
   - Hook line (a specific result or a sharp observation)
   - Who they help and the problem
   - How they do it (method, in plain words)
   - Proof (only numbers/credentials from the fundamentals)
   - One-line call to action


Match the voice notes in the fundamentals. No emoji walls. No "passionate about". No "results-driven".

4. Micro-Offer DM Scripts

You are writing cold outbound DMs for a service business.

CLIENT FUNDAMENTALS:
{{FUNDAMENTALS}}
TARGET AUDIENCE: {{AUDIENCE}}
THE OFFER: {{MICRO_OFFER}}


Write a 4-message LinkedIn DM sequence:

  • Message 1: connection-request note, under 280 characters, references something specific about the prospect type, no pitch.
  • Message 2 (day 2): one-line observation about a problem this audience has, ends with a soft question.
  • Message 3 (day 5): the micro-offer framed as a low-friction next step.
  • Message 4 (day 9): one-line breakup, leaves the door open.

Each message under 60 words. Conversational, no corporate tone, no "I hope this finds you well". Give two variants of Message 1.

5. SOP Writer

You are documenting a repeatable process so any team member can run it without you.

RAW PROCESS (transcript, voice note, or rough steps):
{{PROCESS_NOTES}}


Produce an SOP in Markdown:

  1. Title (verb-first, e.g. "Onboard a New Content Client")
  2. When to run this / trigger
  3. Who owns it
  4. Tools and access needed
  5. Numbered steps (each step starts with an action verb, names the tool, and states the done-state)
  6. Quality check (3 things that must be true before this is "done")
  7. Common failure points and the fix

Rules:

  • If a step is ambiguous in the raw notes, write "DECISION NEEDED: [the question]".
  • No step should assume knowledge the raw notes do not contain.

sections.title: Bonus: the capacity prompt
sections.html:
The question every agency owner gets wrong under pressure is "can we take this next client without dropping a ball." Run this before you say yes.

You are an ops lead checking whether the agency can absorb a new client.

CURRENT LOAD:

  • Active clients: {{N}}
  • Hours/week each active client consumes (list): {{HOURS_LIST}}
  • Team members and their weekly available hours: {{TEAM}}
  • New client estimated weekly hours: {{NEW_CLIENT_HOURS}}

Return:

  1. Current utilization % per team member.
  2. Total spare capacity in hours/week.
  3. Verdict: TAKE IT / TAKE IT WITH ONE CHANGE / DO NOT TAKE IT YET.
  4. If "with one change", name the single highest-impact move (delegate X, automate Y, push start date Z).
Show the math in one short table.

Why it earns its place: the binding constraint on a growing agency is delivery capacity, and it is the number owners track least. One prompt turns a gut call into a defensible one.

sections.title: Wiring it past copy-paste
sections.html:
You can run this stack by hand inside one Claude project today and capture most of the win. When the manual run gets old, the upgrade path is short:

  • Trigger: Google Form submission fires a webhook.
  • Orchestration: an automation layer (n8n or similar) maps form fields into the {{INTAKE}} block and calls Claude once per prompt.
  • Delivery: outputs land as Google Docs in the client's existing folder, and a task drops into your ClickUp board for review.
Start manual, prove the prompts produce a first cut you trust, then automate the plumbing. Automating a prompt you have not tuned just generates wrong documents faster.

That sequencing matters. The prompts are the asset. The wiring is the convenience.

Run the five prompts against your last client's intake form, then send me the two documents that still needed the most editing and I will tune those prompts for your voice: Get in Touch.
